prompt_free_text:
This paper studies sample efficiency in safe reinforcement learning and proposes ESPO, a primal-style safe policy optimization method that adaptively changes the number of samples collected per iteration based on the conflict between reward and safety gradients. The method builds on a three-mode optimization scheme: optimize cost only under clear safety violation, optimize reward only when comfortably safe, and optimize a reward-cost combination in a soft-constraint region, with larger sample sizes used when reward and safety gradients conflict. The paper also claims convergence guarantees, reduced oscillation relative to CRPO, and improved sample complexity, and reports empirical gains on Safety-MuJoCo and Omnisafe benchmarks.

Overall, the paper addresses an important and underexplored question. Sample efficiency is indeed a major bottleneck in safe RL, and the idea of adapting sampling effort to the local difficulty of balancing reward and safety is intuitively appealing. The use of gradient conflict as a signal is also natural in constrained or multi-objective optimization. The empirical results, if robust, suggest that the approach may be practically useful. However, in its current form, I have substantial concerns about the technical clarity, correctness of the algorithm description, strength of the theoretical claims, and completeness/fairness of the empirical evaluation. My assessment is therefore mixed: the paper has a promising core idea, but the presentation and validation are not yet at the standard expected for a top-tier ML venue.

The main strength of the paper is the problem framing. Existing safe RL methods often use a fixed rollout budget per update, and it is plausible that this is wasteful in easy phases and insufficient in difficult phases. Bringing adaptive sampling ideas from stochastic optimization into safe RL is a worthwhile direction. The paper also makes a reasonable design choice in using the reward-cost gradient angle as a proxy for optimization difficulty. In the soft-constraint region, increasing sample size when gradients conflict and decreasing it otherwise is conceptually sensible. Another positive aspect is that the method is built on top of an existing primal framework rather than requiring a wholly new safe RL formulation, which may make it easier to adopt in practice.

That said, the paper currently suffers from a serious issue of algorithmic ambiguity. The description of the update rules in Section 4.3 appears inconsistent with Section 4.1. In Section 4.1, Equation (3) is used when gradients conflict and Equation (4) when they are aligned. But in Section 4.3, the text seems to reverse these cases: for gradient angle less than or equal to 90 degrees it says the policy is updated according to Equation (3), and for angle greater than 90 degrees according to Equation (4). This is not a minor typo, because it changes the actual algorithmic behavior. If this is only a writing mistake, it must be corrected everywhere; if not, then the method as implemented may differ from the method analyzed. More broadly, the practical algorithm is deferred to the appendix, but the main paper does not specify enough details to make the method reproducible: how exactly are gradients estimated, how are the weights x_t^r and x_t^c chosen, how are h^- and h^+ set in practice, how are the sample adjustment parameters zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- computed, bounded, or scheduled, and what minimum/maximum sample sizes are enforced? Without these details, the contribution remains underspecified.

The sample manipulation mechanism itself is also too abstractly defined. Equations (6) and (7) only state that the sample size is X + X zeta_t^+ or X + X zeta_t^-, depending on conflict. But the paper never gives a concrete rule for zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- in the main text. Are they constants, functions of the angle, functions of gradient norms, or learned quantities? If they are hyperparameters, how many are there and how sensitive is performance to them? Since the claimed contribution is specifically adaptive sample sizing, the adaptation rule should be central and explicit. As written, the paper establishes only a high-level principle, not a fully specified algorithm.

I also found the theoretical section significantly weaker than the paper claims. The convergence theorem is stated only for a tabular CMDP with softmax policies and appears to rely on natural policy gradient style assumptions and policy evaluation subroutines. This is a very limited setting relative to the deep continuous-control experiments used later. The gap between theory and practice is therefore large. That is not necessarily fatal, but the paper should be much more careful in how it presents the theory. In particular, the theorem seems to establish a convergence rate comparable to CRPO, not a stronger one. The claimed novelty is then not convergence speed in iterations, but reduced sample usage via adaptive batch sizes. Yet Proposition 4.3, which is supposed to formalize sample efficiency, is stated only qualitatively: ESPO “needs fewer number of samples” than the version without sample manipulation to achieve target gaps. No explicit bound is shown in the main text, no dependence on conflict frequency or zeta parameters is given, and no quantitative improvement factor is visible. As a result, the proposition reads more like an informal statement than a substantive theorem. For a paper centered on sample complexity, this is a major weakness.

Similarly, Proposition 4.2 on reduced oscillation is interesting in spirit but raises questions. The proposition says that once ESPO enters the safe region up to h^+, it stays there and continues to optimize reward at least partially. This sounds strong, but the statement depends on “adaptively choosing” the parameters x_t^r and x_t^c, which may make the result somewhat existential rather than constructive. It is unclear whether the practical algorithm actually computes such choices, and under what assumptions this no-oscillation property holds in stochastic settings with estimated gradients. Since the empirical motivation is reduced oscillation due to adaptive sampling, but the proposition seems more tied to the three-mode update structure inherited from PCRPO, the paper should disentangle what benefit comes from the optimization mode design and what benefit comes specifically from sample manipulation.

The empirical section is encouraging but not yet convincing enough. The paper reports better reward, safety, and fewer samples than several baselines on Safety-MuJoCo and Omnisafe tasks. However, the evaluation lacks several details needed to assess fairness. First, it is not clear whether all methods are compared under equal wall-clock budgets, equal environment interaction budgets, or equal numbers of policy updates. Since ESPO changes sample counts dynamically, comparisons can easily become confounded. Second, the paper emphasizes that baselines use fixed totals such as 8M or 10M samples while ESPO uses fewer, but it is not clear how stopping is determined for ESPO. Does ESPO stop when performance plateaus, when a fixed number of updates is reached, or when it exhausts a dynamic budget? If baselines are simply run to a fixed maximum while ESPO terminates earlier, then the comparison should also include performance at matched sample budgets and matched training times. Third, the paper repeatedly claims improved safety, but the main text does not provide enough quantitative summaries of constraint violation rates, average episodic costs, or worst-case violations. Curves are referenced, but the review text alone suggests mostly qualitative interpretation.

Another concern is the choice and breadth of baselines. Since ESPO is built directly on PCRPO-style three-mode optimization, the most important ablation is against the exact same optimizer without adaptive sample sizing, under identical implementation details. Proposition 4.3 even refers to such a comparison, but the main experimental section does not foreground it. Comparing against CRPO and PCRPO is useful, but to isolate the contribution of sample manipulation, the paper needs a clean ablation: same update rule, same architecture, same hyperparameters, fixed sample size versus adaptive sample size. The current presentation makes it difficult to tell whether gains come from sample adaptation, from implementation differences, from tuning effort, or from the underlying PCRPO-style gradient handling. Likewise, comparisons to primal-dual methods are interesting, but because these methods have different optimization structures and may have different implementation maturity across benchmarks, they are less diagnostic of the paper’s core contribution.

The paper also needs stronger statistical reporting. I did not see clear mention in the main text of the number of random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing. For RL, especially safe RL, variance across seeds can be substantial. Claims such as “significantly outperforms” and “25–29% fewer samples” should be backed by error bars and statistical summaries. It would also help to report final reward, final cost, area under the reward curve, area under the violation curve, and sample-to-threshold metrics. Right now, the evidence appears suggestive rather than definitive.

There are also conceptual questions about the gradient-conflict criterion. In on-policy deep RL, gradient estimates are noisy, especially for cost signals that may be sparse or high variance. The angle between estimated reward and cost gradients may therefore be unstable. The paper does not discuss whether the angle is smoothed across iterations, whether confidence in the angle estimate is considered, or whether sample size adaptation itself creates a circular dependency: one needs enough samples to estimate whether more samples are needed. This issue is central to the method. A more principled treatment might estimate uncertainty in the conflict signal or use a sequential test before increasing/decreasing rollout counts. At minimum, the paper should discuss robustness of the angle criterion under noisy gradient estimation and provide ablations on threshold choices, e.g., whether 90 degrees is optimal or whether a margin is needed.

The practical overhead of the method is also underexplored. The paper claims reduced training time despite computing both reward and cost gradients and their angle. But in many policy gradient implementations, estimating separate gradients and dynamically changing rollout lengths can introduce nontrivial overhead and engineering complexity. The paper should report not only environment samples and wall-clock time, but also number of updates, average batch size per mode, fraction of iterations in each mode, and computational overhead per update. This is especially important because some baselines may be disadvantaged by implementation differences in the benchmark frameworks.

The writing quality is below conference standard and materially affects readability. There are many grammatical issues, awkward passive constructions, duplicated citations, and notation inconsistencies. Some examples are minor, but others are substantive, such as the mode/update mismatch noted above. The paper also occasionally overstates claims. For example, saying ESPO “achieves convergence to a globally optimal policy” based on a tabular theorem with randomized output and hidden constants is too strong. The theory supports a rate bound under restrictive assumptions, not a broad practical guarantee for the deep RL setting. The manuscript would benefit from careful editing for precision and correctness.

I think the paper could become much stronger with targeted revisions. First, the algorithm must be fully and unambiguously specified in the main paper. The exact adaptive sample-size rule should be explicit, including how zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- are computed, clipped, and tuned. The mismatch between Sections 4.1 and 4.3 must be fixed. Second, the theory should either provide a genuinely quantitative sample complexity improvement or tone down the claims. If Proposition 4.3 has a concrete bound in the appendix, that bound should be summarized in the main text with clear dependence on relevant quantities. Third, the experiments should include a direct ablation against the same base optimizer without adaptive sampling, matched-budget comparisons, seed counts with confidence intervals, and more detailed safety metrics. Fourth, the paper should analyze sensitivity to the conflict threshold, soft-constraint band parameters, and sample adjustment hyperparameters. Fifth, the authors should discuss the reliability of gradient-angle estimation under stochastic noise and perhaps compare against simpler adaptive heuristics, such as increasing sample size based on gradient variance or recent constraint oscillation, to show that conflict-awareness is specifically beneficial.

In terms of novelty, I would characterize the contribution as moderate. Adaptive sampling itself is not new, and gradient conflict handling in reward-safety optimization is also not new due to PCRPO and related multi-objective gradient surgery ideas. The novel combination is to use reward-cost conflict to drive adaptive rollout size in safe RL. That is a reasonable contribution, but it needs sharper technical and empirical substantiation to justify strong claims.

My overall recommendation is currently negative, though not by a large margin. The paper has a promising idea and some encouraging results, but the current version does not yet provide the level of rigor, clarity, and validation needed for acceptance at a top-tier venue. With a clearer algorithm, stronger and more transparent theory, and more careful experiments isolating the effect of adaptive sampling, this line of work could become a solid contribution.

The main questions I would want the authors to address are: What is the exact adaptive rule for sample size, and how sensitive is it? Is the algorithm description in Sections 4.1 and 4.3 consistent with the implementation? Can the authors provide a quantitative sample complexity improvement theorem rather than a qualitative proposition? How does ESPO compare to the same three-mode optimizer with fixed sample size under matched update counts, matched sample budgets, and matched wall-clock time? How noisy is the gradient-angle estimate in practice, and does smoothing or confidence-aware estimation matter? And finally, can the authors provide stronger statistical evidence and more detailed safety metrics across seeds?

In summary, the paper tackles an important problem with an intuitively appealing approach, but the current manuscript leaves too many key details unresolved and does not yet convincingly establish its claims.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes Efficient Safe Policy Optimization (ESPO), a safe RL method that augments a three-mode primal optimization framework with adaptive sample-size manipulation based on reward-cost gradient conflict. The method uses three update regimes: cost-only when constraints are violated, reward-only when safely feasible, and joint reward/cost optimization in a soft-constraint region, with projected gradients under conflict. The main claimed contribution is to increase sample size when reward and safety gradients conflict and decrease it otherwise, aiming to improve sample efficiency and reduce oscillation near the safety boundary. The paper provides a tabular softmax-policy analysis claiming convergence rates comparable to CRPO, reduced oscillation relative to CRPO, and fewer samples than a non-adaptive variant. Empirically, ESPO is evaluated on Safety-MuJoCo and Omnisafe tasks against primal and primal-dual baselines, with reported gains in reward, safety, sample usage, and training time.
strengths: Addresses an important problem: improving sample efficiency in safe RL while maintaining constraint satisfaction.
The intuition of using reward-cost gradient conflict to modulate optimization behavior is reasonable and connects to prior work in multi-objective optimization and safe RL.
Builds on an existing three-mode primal framework and attempts to unify optimization behavior and adaptive sampling in a simple algorithmic design.
Includes both theoretical and empirical components, with experiments on two commonly used safe RL benchmark suites.
Reports practical metrics beyond reward, including safety behavior, sample count, and training time, which are relevant for safe RL.
weaknesses: The core adaptive sampling mechanism is underspecified: the paper introduces sample sizes as X(1+zeta_t^+) or X(1+zeta_t^-) but does not define how zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- are computed, bounded, or tuned in practice, making the method difficult to reproduce and weakening the claimed novelty.

There is a serious inconsistency between the textual description and the algorithm mapping in Section 4.3: for soft constraint violations with angle <= 90 degrees, the text says Equation (7) is used for sample adjustment and Equation (3) for policy update, while Equation (3) was earlier defined for conflict (angle > 90 degrees); similarly the >90-degree case is paired with Equation (4), contradicting Section 4.1. This suggests either a substantive algorithmic error or a major presentation flaw.

The theoretical claims about sample efficiency are extremely weak as stated. Proposition 4.3 only says ESPO needs fewer samples than a version without sample manipulation, but no explicit sample complexity bound, dependence on problem parameters, or conditions under which the comparison holds are provided in the main text.

The convergence theorem is only for a tabular softmax setting, whereas experiments are in deep continuous-control benchmarks. The gap between theory and practice is large and not convincingly bridged.

The paper repeatedly claims improved safety and reward, but the main text provides only qualitative references to figures and sample-count tables; numerical statistics, variance across seeds, significance testing, and exact safety violation summaries are largely absent from the provided content.

Comparison fairness is unclear because ESPO uses fewer total samples than baselines by design, yet reward/safety comparisons may depend strongly on training horizon. It is not clear whether baselines were also evaluated at matched sample budgets or whether ESPO simply stops earlier.

The method appears closely tied to PCRPO, with ESPO essentially adding adaptive sample sizing on top of PCRPO-style three-mode updates. The incremental novelty over PCRPO is therefore moderate unless the adaptive sampling theory and implementation are especially strong, which they currently are not.
The writing contains many grammatical issues and several notation/presentation problems, reducing clarity and confidence in the technical correctness.
methodological_flaws: Algorithmic inconsistency: Section 4.1 defines Equation (3) for conflicting gradients (angle > 90 degrees) and Equation (4) for aligned gradients (angle <= 90 degrees), but Section 4.3 reverses these assignments when describing the practical algorithm. This is not a minor typo because it changes the actual update rule used in the key regime.

The sample manipulation rule is not operationally specified. Without a definition of zeta_t^+ and zeta_t^- or a criterion linking gradient conflict magnitude to sample size, the method cannot be verified or reproduced, and the theoretical claims cannot be meaningfully assessed against the implemented algorithm.

Theorem 4.1 appears to establish essentially the same convergence rate as CRPO in a tabular setting, so it does not theoretically justify the claimed practical sample-efficiency gains in deep RL. The theorem concerns iteration complexity under policy evaluation assumptions, not environment interaction complexity in the experimental setting.

Proposition 4.2 claims ESPO can remain in the safe/soft region without oscillation by adaptively choosing weights (x_t^r, x_t^c), but the existence and construction of such weights may be nontrivial and potentially problem-dependent. As stated, the proposition risks being existential rather than algorithmically guaranteed.

Proposition 4.3 is too vague to support the headline claim of improved sample complexity bounds. It provides no explicit bound, no quantitative improvement factor, and no assumptions under which the comparison is valid. As written, it is closer to an informal comparative statement than a rigorous theorem.

Empirical validity is weakened by insufficient reporting detail in the main text: number of seeds, confidence intervals, exact hyperparameter tuning protocol, matched compute/sample budgets, and statistical significance are not clearly presented here. This makes it difficult to assess whether the reported 25-29% sample savings and 21-38% training-time reductions are robust.

The comparison against primal-dual methods may be confounded by implementation/framework differences and by the fact that ESPO is built on a different optimization paradigm. Without careful budget matching and tuning transparency, superiority claims are not fully convincing.
